t: Kth Smallest Subarray Sum — Binary Search on the Answer
o: Every non-empty contiguous window contributes one sum, so there are n(n+1)/2 of them — about 2*10^8 for n = 2*10^4, far too many to enumerate or sort. All elements are positive, meaning extending a window never decreases its sum; this monotonicity lets us answer "how many subarray sums are at most x?" in linear time with a sliding window, and that count grows monotonically with x. In Example 1 the ordered sums are 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, so the 4th smallest is 3; in Example 2 the ordering ends ..., 8, 10, 11, 13, 16 and the 7th is 10. Binary searching x over [min(nums), sum(nums)] finds the smallest value whose count reaches k, which is exactly the k-th smallest subarray sum.
k: With strictly positive elements, the number of subarrays whose sum is at most x is computable in O(n) by sliding a window.
count(sum <= x) is non-decreasing in x, so the k-th smallest sum is found by binary searching the value domain.
The converged value is always an achievable subarray sum: it is the smallest x where the count first reaches k.

a.i: Fix each start index, extend the end while accumulating a running sum, and collect all n(n+1)/2 values; then select the k-th smallest. This restates the definition exactly and works as a correctness oracle, but materializing hundreds of millions of sums violates both time and memory limits at the top constraints.
s: Iterate start i from 0 to n-1 with running sum cur = 0.
For each end j >= i add nums[j] to cur and store cur.
Select the k-th smallest from the collected multiset (sort or quickselect).
a.t: O(n^2) sums plus selection — about 2*10^8 values at n = 2*10^4; sorting adds a log factor

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search the Value + Sliding Window Count
a.i: Define countAtMost(limit): sweep the right end while shrinking the left whenever the running sum exceeds limit; because elements are positive, each valid window ending at right is counted once via right - left + 1. This count is non-decreasing in limit, so binary search the smallest limit with count >= k — that limit is the k-th smallest sum. Roughly 40 iterations of an O(n) sweep handle the full constraint range comfortably.
s: While lo < hi, take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2).
Compute cnt = number of subarrays with sum <= mid using a sliding window.
If cnt >= k set hi = mid, else set lo = mid + 1.
a.t: O(n log S) — about log(sum) ≈ 40 binary-search rounds, each an O(n) window sweep
a.sp: O(1) — only scalar accumulators beyond the input

w: State the positivity requirement explicitly — the sliding window count silently breaks with negatives. Pitfalls: overflowing 32-bit sums in Java/C++ (total reaches 10^9, and lo+hi intermediates exceed int); counting windows per left endpoint instead of per right endpoint; assuming the binary-searched value might be unachievable — the invariant guarantees it equals some subarray sum. Follow-up: with negative numbers allowed, pair prefix sums with a merge-sort or BIT-based counting, or find the k-th smallest range-sum among all pairs of sorted prefix lists with a heap.
